items.title: Ukrainian drones strike major Russian Baltic export port
points: Ukraine has launched a major drone attack on Russia’s Baltic port of Ust-Luga, setting fire to port infrastructure, injuring three workers and disrupting power supplies.
Leningrad region governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed early Wednesday that several drones had struck the port area, triggering a fire and an emergency shutdown of a transformer substation.
Ust-Luga is among Russia’s most important Baltic export gateways, handling crude oil, refined petroleum products, coal, grain and other bulk commodities.
The attack comes just two days after Ukrainian drones hit the Kirishi refinery, Russia’s second-largest, also in the Leningrad region.
The Surgutneftegaz-operated facility, which has annual processing capacity of around 20m tonnes, caught fire following Monday’s attack.
The latest Baltic attack follows another violent weekend in the Black Sea.
Splash reported on Monday that Russia had claimed fresh attacks on merchant ships around Odesa and Chornomorsk, although the incidents could not be independently verified.

items.title: Rice prices rise amid lower expected production, inadequate rainfall, reduced fertilizer use
points: Rice prices have been rising in the domestic market amid expectations of lower production in the 2026-27 crop year (July-June), as inadequate rainfall and reduced fertiliser application are likely to affect yields from the paddy crop currently being harvested.
Paddy prices in Kota, Rajasthan, have risen to ₹4,500-4,700 per quintal from ₹3,200-3,400 a year ago, according to mandi trader Aniket Mehta.

The average all-India retail price of rice was ₹49 per kg on November 10, nearly 14% higher than ₹42.96 per kg a year ago and 7% above ₹45.81 per kg a month ago, according to Department of Consumer Affairs data.
The Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO) All Rice Price Index averaged 112.3 points in October, up 1.6% from September.

Indian exporters anticipate possible restrictions on exports of 100% broken white rice amid higher domestic prices and increased demand from these sectors, S&P Global Energy reported on November 6, citing industry sources.

items.title: Coal’s new world order takes shape
points: Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured.
Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes.
Beneath that modest increase, Indonesian exports are projected to fall 6% to 496.9m tonnes, while Australian shipments climb 4% to 371.3m tonnes.
Chinese seaborne imports are expected to decline 5%, India’s 3%, while Japan’s rise 3%.
Braemar’s analysis of AXSMarine tracking shows exports falling 8% year-on-year during January-October.
Ursa Shipbrokers calculates combined South African and Mozambican steam coal exports reached a ten-year high of 64.92m tonnes during January-October, with 27.26m tonnes destined for India.
Supramaxes have been hardest hit, with Indian-bound coal volumes falling 16%, compared with a 4% decline for panamaxes.
October offered the first signs of a turn, with Indian seaborne coal arrivals rising 7% year-on-year.

items.title: China Merchants revives another shipyard
points: China Merchants is moving to take control of the long-dormant Quanzhou Shipyard in Fujian province, the latest in a string of yard revivals that has seen China’s shipbuilding capacity nearly double in recent years.

The state-owned conglomerate has signed a strategic cooperation agreement with Quanzhou authorities, paving the way for the revival of a facility whose newbuilding operations have been largely idle for more than a decade.
The yard occupies 134 hectares, with 3.6 km of coastline and two drydocks capable of accommodating 300,000 dwt vessels.
Repair operations resumed in 2023, but a return to large-scale shipbuilding would represent a significant expansion.
China Merchants has already absorbed or reactivated yards in Qingdao, Nanjing and Wuhan over the past 18 months.
Clarksons Research revealed this month that the global orderbook had reached a record 226.1m compensated gross tonnes (cgt), surpassing the previous peak of 225.5m cgt set in September 2008.
Worth approximately $700bn, the backlog is heavily concentrated in China, whose yards control 68% of outstanding orders.

items.title: Panama Canal turns the taps back on
points: The Panama Canal has raised its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and increased the maximum allowable draft for neopanamax ships to 50 ft, marking another significant easing of restrictions following an exceptionally wet October.
The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) confirmed that an additional booking slot for super-category vessels at the original panamax locks would increase their daily allocation from 18 to 19.
